rewritten_text:
No letter of sympathy had been sent to Ireland. That neglect had been repaid in kind: when poor Lady Elliot herself died, no condolences reached Kellynch. There was therefore considerable reason to fear that the Dalrymples regarded the family connection as ended. The pressing question was how to repair the damage and be accepted as cousins again. In a more sensible way, neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot considered that question unimportant. Family ties were worth maintaining, and good society was worth cultivating. Lady Dalrymple had rented a house in Laura Place for three months and intended to entertain in style. She had visited Bath the previous year, when Lady Russell had heard her described as a charming woman. Renewing the connection was highly desirable, provided the Elliots could do so without compromising their dignity.

Sir Walter, however, insisted on choosing his own approach. Eventually he sent his distinguished cousin an elaborate letter full of explanations, regrets, and appeals. Neither Lady Russell nor Mr Elliot could admire it, but it achieved everything intended: the Dowager Viscountess replied in three scribbled lines that she felt greatly honoured and would be delighted to know them. The hard work was over; now came the rewards. They called at Laura Place. They received the visiting cards of the Dowager Viscountess Dalrymple and the Honourable Miss Carteret, which could be displayed wherever they would attract most attention. Everyone heard about 'our cousins in Laura Place' and 'our cousin Lady Dalrymple and Miss Carteret.'

Anne was embarrassed. Even if Lady Dalrymple and her daughter had been delightful, Anne would still have been ashamed of all this excitement. But they were entirely unremarkable. Neither manners, accomplishments, nor intelligence distinguished them. Lady Dalrymple had earned her reputation as 'a charming woman' by offering everyone a smile and a polite answer. Miss Carteret had even less to say and was so unattractive and awkward that, without her birth, she would never have been tolerated in Camden Place.

Lady Russell admitted that she had expected more, yet continued to regard them as acquaintances worth having. When Anne ventured to share her opinion with Mr Elliot, he agreed that they had no particular merits themselves. Nevertheless, as relatives, as members of good society, and as people who would attract good society around them, they possessed value. Anne smiled and replied,

'My idea of good company, Mr Elliot, is intelligent, well-informed people with plenty to talk about. That is what I mean by good company.'

I cannot understand why she ever wanted to be close to me. Still, if it all happened again, I am sure I would be taken in again. Caroline did not return my visit until yesterday, and in all that time I received not a single note or line from her. When she finally came, she clearly took no pleasure in it. She offered a brief, formal apology for not visiting sooner, said nothing about wanting to see me again, and seemed so completely changed that by the time she left, I had firmly decided to end the friendship. I feel sorry for her, although I cannot help blaming her too. She was wrong to single me out as she did. I can honestly say that every step toward friendship began with her. But I pity her because she must know she has behaved badly, and because I am sure concern for her brother explains it. I need not say more. We know she has nothing to worry about, but if she does worry, that would easily explain her treatment of me. Her brother deserves her affection, and any concern she feels for him is natural and kind. Even so, I wonder why she still has these fears. If he had cared for me at all, we would have met long ago. Something she said convinced me that he knows I am in town. Yet the way she spoke suggested that she was trying to convince herself he really prefers Miss Darcy. I cannot understand it. If I were not afraid of judging too harshly, I would almost say that the whole affair looks very dishonest. I will try to put every painful thought aside and think only of what makes me happy: your love, and our dear uncle and aunt's constant kindness. Please write very soon. Miss Bingley mentioned that her brother might never return to Netherfield and might give up the house, though she sounded uncertain. We had better say nothing about it. I am so glad you have had such pleasant news from our friends at Hunsford. Do go and visit them with Sir William and Maria. I am sure you will be very comfortable there.

"Yours, etc."

The letter distressed Elizabeth, but she felt better when she reflected that at least the sister would no longer deceive Jane. By now, all hope connected with the brother had completely ended.

His intellect and temperament, although different from her own, would have fulfilled all her wishes. Their marriage would surely have benefited them both. Her warmth and liveliness might have softened his outlook and improved his manners, while his judgment, knowledge, and worldly experience would have offered her still more significant advantages.

But no such happy marriage could now demonstrate true marital happiness to an admiring audience. A very different union was about to take place within their family, one that ruled out any possibility of the other.

She could not imagine how Wickham and Lydia would support themselves with any reasonable independence. She could, however, easily imagine how little lasting happiness awaited a couple brought together only because desire had proved stronger than principle.

Mr. Gardiner soon wrote to his brother again. He briefly answered Mr. Bennet's thanks, assuring him that he was eager to help any member of the family and begging him never to mention the subject again. The main purpose of his letter was to announce that Mr. Wickham had decided to leave the militia.

"I very much wanted him to take that step," he added, "as soon as the marriage was agreed upon. I believe you will agree that leaving his present corps is highly advisable, both for him and for my niece. Mr. Wickham plans to join the regular army, and some of his former friends are still willing and able to help him there. He has been promised a commission as an ensign in General----'s regiment, currently stationed in the north. Its distance from this part of the country is an advantage. His promises sound encouraging, and I hope that among new people, with reputations of their own to protect, they will both behave more responsibly. I have written to Colonel Forster to explain our arrangements and ask him to reassure Mr. Wickham's various creditors in and around Brighton that they will soon be paid. I have personally guaranteed that payment. Would you take the trouble to give his creditors in Meryton the same assurance? I will include a list based on the information he has supplied. He has declared all his debts; at least, I hope he has not deceived us. Haggerston has our instructions, and everything will be completed within a week. They will then travel to his regiment unless they receive an invitation to Longbourn first. Mrs. Gardiner tells me that my niece is very eager to see you all before she leaves the south.
